title: The Nurses and the Phone Order
text:
In the mid 1960s the psychiatrist Charles Hofling and his colleagues set up a quiet test in two American hospitals. A fictitious drug called Astroten was placed in the ward medicine cabinets, labeled with a maximum daily dose of 10 milligrams. Then, during an evening shift, a man phoned the nurse on duty, introduced himself as a doctor she had never heard of, and asked her to give a patient 20 milligrams right away. He said he was in a hurry and would sign the order when he arrived.

The request broke several hospital rules at once: orders were not to be taken by phone, the doctor was unknown, the drug was not on the approved list, and the dose was twice the stated limit. Yet 21 of the 22 nurses who received the call were stopped by an observer on their way to the patient with the medicine in hand. When other nurses were asked what they would do in the same situation, nearly all said they would refuse.

Eleven years later, Steven Rank and Cardell Jacobson repeated the idea with an important difference. The drug was the familiar Valium, and the nurses were free to talk to colleagues before acting. This time only 2 of 18 prepared to give the overdose.
lesson: Rank and confident tone can override training and rules. Leaders should build systems where questioning an order is normal, and where people have the knowledge and the colleagues to check it.
people: Charles Hofling and colleagues; Steven Rank and Cardell Jacobson (1977 follow-up)
source: Hofling, C. K., Brotzman, E., Dalrymple, S., Graves, N., and Pierce, C. M. (1966). An experimental study in nurse-physician relationships. Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease, 143(2), 171-180.
